title: Climbing Lenin Peak: Full Guide
excerpt: Lenin Peak, 7,134 m, is one of the most accessible peaks above 7,000 m. The full guide: the camps, acclimatization, summit day, gear, experience, entry to Kyrgyzstan and season.
seoTitle: Climbing Lenin Peak: Route, Camps, Experience and Cost

content.value: On day 15 of the expedition, from Camp 3 at 6,100 m, climbers set out on their longest day: the ascent to the summit of Lenin Peak, 7,134 m (23,406 ft), in the Pamir on the border between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, and the return to the tents. Lenin Peak is considered one of the most accessible mountains in the world above 7,000 m, and for many it is their first summit at that height. It is not a very technical climb, but it requires previous experience above 5,500 m, glacier travel with crampons, ice axe and ropes, very high endurance and the patience of a 20-day expedition. The season is summer, in July and August.

This guide gathers what you need to know before you decide: what makes the mountain serious, how the route works camp by camp, how acclimatization works, what happens on summit day, what gear and experience are required, what it takes to enter Kyrgyzstan and the border zone, and when to go. If you have already stood on a high summit and are asking yourself whether 7,000 meters is the next step, this is where to start.
What makes Lenin Peak a serious mountain

Lenin Peak rises to 7,134 m in the Trans-Alai Range, in the northern part of the Pamir mountains in Central Asia. The summit sits on the border between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, and on the Tajik side it is called Ibn Sina Peak. It is the highest summit of the range, and of all the mountains above 7,000 m, it is the one climbed by the most people. The reason is simple: its normal route is considered one of the least technical among mountains of this height.

Less technical does not mean easy. The route crosses the Lenin Glacier, which has crevassed areas, so you walk it roped together. On the way to Camp 2 there is a steep slope exposed to avalanches after heavy snowfall, and above 6,000 m wind and cold are part of every day. But the main danger on the mountain is the altitude itself. Altitude sickness is the central threat, and evacuation options from the high camps are limited and slow. That is why the whole itinerary is built around patient acclimatization.

content.title: ✦ The longest day
content.value: On summit day you climb from Camp 3, at 6,100 m, to the summit at 7,134 m, and return to the same camp. That is a difference of more than 1,000 m at an altitude where every step has a price, which makes it the longest and hardest day of the expedition.
Osh and Achik Tash Base Camp

The expedition starts in Osh, in southern Kyrgyzstan. On the first day you land in Osh, and from there you transfer the same day to Achik Tash Base Camp, at 3,600 m. Airport transfers and internal transfers are included in the price, as is one night in a hotel in Osh with breakfast. Lunch and dinner at the hotel are not included.

Achik Tash is home to the expedition in the first days, on the rest days in the middle and at the end of the climb. You sleep there in tents, as throughout the climb, and use of showers, toilets, laundry and electricity at the camps is included in the price. Anyone who wants to upgrade to a yurt, the traditional felt tent of the Central Asian nomads, or to enjoy a sauna can do so at extra cost. Porters carry up to 25 kg of personal gear per participant to Base Camp, and three full meals a day are included throughout the climb.

On days 2 and 3 you stay at Base Camp and begin acclimatizing. On day 2 you hike to a waterfall, and on day 3 you make an acclimatization climb to Petrovsky Ridge, at 4,850 m, and come back to sleep at 3,600 m.

content.value: The route, camp by camp
Above Base Camp there are three high camps. In our itinerary they are called Camp 1 (4,400 m), Camp 2 (5,300 m) and Camp 3 (6,100 m), and the summit attempt starts from Camp 3.
Camp 1, 4,400 m

The way from Base Camp crosses a mountain pass and a valley, then continues along the moraine, the band of rocks and gravel at the edge of the Lenin Glacier, to Camp 1. It is a long walking day. Camp 1 is the acclimatization base on the mountain: on day 5 you climb from it to the summit of Yukhin, 5,100 m, and come back to sleep there, and on day 6 it hosts ice training and preparations for the climb. From here up, porters carry up to 15 kg of personal gear per participant between the camps.
Camp 2, 5,300 m

Between Camp 1 and Camp 2 lies one of the most demanding sections of the route. You cross the Lenin Glacier, and in the crevassed area you walk roped together. Further on you climb a steep snow wall, and after it you cross a wide glacier basin that climbers call the Frying Pan: during the day the sun reflected off the snow makes it especially hot, and the slopes above it are exposed to avalanches after heavy snowfall. That is why you set out on this section early in the morning, when the snow is harder and more stable. Camp 2 sits on a rocky outcrop at the side of the glacier.
Camp 3, 6,100 m

From Camp 2 you climb a broad ridge, steep at its start and at its end, to Camp 3, which lies close to Razdelnaya Peak (6,148 m). This is the high camp of the expedition, and it is exposed to the wind. In our itinerary you reach it twice: the first time to touch the altitude and descend to sleep at Camp 2, and the second time on the eve of summit day.
Summit day

Summit day starts before sunrise. From Camp 3 you descend a little to a saddle, and from there the long ridge that leads to the summit begins. Its lower part has a steep, exposed section where fixed ropes are usually installed during the season. Above it the ridge widens, and long plateaus lead to the summit, 7,134 m. The summit itself is flat, and in fog or cloud it is hard to identify and to navigate along the ridge.

Such a day usually lasts between 10 and 15 hours up and down, and sometimes longer. The summit is only halfway: after it you descend the whole ridge and climb back up the short stretch you descended in the morning, back to Camp 3, where you sleep. Only the next day do you descend to Camp 1. That is why you reach the summit with enough strength and time in hand to come down safely, and the judgment of the guides decides when to turn back.
Our expedition, day by day
The HighAir Lenin Peak expedition lasts 20 days, from arrival in Osh to the flight home. This is the itinerary:

items: Day 1: arrival in Osh and transfer to Achik Tash Base Camp (3,600 m).
Day 2: acclimatization day at Base Camp and hike to a waterfall.
Day 3: acclimatization climb to Petrovsky Ridge (4,850 m).
Day 4: ascent from Base Camp to Camp 1 (4,400 m).
Day 5: climb to the summit of Yukhin (5,100 m) and back to Camp 1.
Day 6: ice training and climbing preparations at Camp 1.
Day 8: ascent to Camp 3 (6,100 m) and back to sleep at Camp 2.
Day 9: descent from Camp 2 to Base Camp (3,600 m).
Days 10 and 11: rest and preparation at Base Camp.
Day 12: ascent from Base Camp to Camp 1 (4,400 m).
Day 15: summit day, ascent of Lenin Peak (7,134 m) and back to Camp 3.
Day 16: descent from Camp 3 to Camp 1 (4,400 m).
Day 17: descent from Camp 1 to Base Camp (3,600 m).
Day 18: spare day for bad weather.
Day 19: transfer back to Osh and a night at the hotel.
Day 20: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: The itinerary is built on the principle of "climb high, sleep low", and on three acclimatization climbs, each higher than the one before. On day 3 you climb to Petrovsky Ridge, 4,850 m, and come back to sleep at 3,600 m. On day 5 you climb Yukhin, 5,100 m, and come back to sleep at 4,400 m. On day 8 you touch 6,100 m at Camp 3 and descend to sleep at 5,300 m. After that rotation you descend all the way to Base Camp for two rest days, in air richer in oxygen, during which the body recovers and completes its acclimatization. When you set out on the summit attempt, the body has already met the altitude of Camp 3 about a week earlier.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse, you descend. The group carries a Magnus satellite device.

content.title: ✦ A spare day for the weather
content.value: Day 18 in the itinerary is a spare day. If the weather delays the summit attempt, the schedule can shift by one day without giving up the summit in advance. Days can also be added, at 50 US dollars per person per day at Base Camp and 150 US dollars per person per day at the high camps.
Technical gear and required experience

Lenin Peak is a mountain of glacier and snow, and technical gear is part of the climb: crampons, ice axe, harness, ropes and carabiners. On the glacier you walk roped together, and on the steep sections you work with the fixed ropes. On day 6, at Camp 1, there is ice training and preparation for the climb before you reach those sections.

Climbing gear is not included in the price of the expedition, nor is personal gear: clothing, footwear and mountaineering boots. Above 6,000 m the cold and wind are strong, so full winter clothing, warm gloves and high-altitude mountain boots are part of safety. Every registered climber receives a full gear list from us, a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call before departure.

Lenin Peak is not a first mountain. Previous experience above 5,500 m is required, for example the summit of Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) or Aconcagua (6,962 m). That experience teaches you how your body reacts to lack of oxygen and to cold, and anyone who has already walked with crampons and an ice axe reaches the glacier with a real advantage. A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join.
Entering Kyrgyzstan and the border zone permit

Citizens of the UK, the US, the EU countries and many others enter Kyrgyzstan without a visa, with a valid passport, for a stay of up to 30 days (as of 2026; the limit was cut from 60 days at the end of 2025). The expedition lasts 20 days, so it fits within that period. Entry rules can change, so check them for your passport before booking and again before you fly.

Base Camp and the road to it lie in a border zone, close to the border with Tajikistan, and entering it requires a border zone permit from the Kyrgyz authorities. The permit is arranged in advance, usually through a licensed local agency, and it requires your passport details and travel dates. At checkpoints on the way, keep your passport and the permit within easy reach. Reserve entry permits and the Lenin Peak climbing permit are included in the price of our expedition.

Travel and medical insurance is not included in the price. Make sure the policy covers climbing to 7,134 m on a glacier, including search, rescue and evacuation, and check your government's current travel advice for Kyrgyzstan before you go. International flights are not included either.
When to climb Lenin Peak

The climbing season on Lenin Peak is short: summer, mainly July and August. In these months the camps at the foot of the mountain operate, and the weather and snow conditions are more stable. May and June are the wetter months, and in September temperatures drop quickly and storms become more frequent. Even in the heart of the season the weather in the Pamir changes fast, and strong winds can close the summit. Our expeditions depart in July and August.
Who it suits

Lenin Peak suits anyone who has already stood on a high summit and wants to cross the 7,000 meter line. For many it is their first summit at that height, and the natural step after Kilimanjaro or Aconcagua. It requires very high endurance, the ability to cope with significant altitude conditions and a readiness for a long stay in the field: about two and a half weeks in tents, with days of waiting, cold and slow work at altitude.

If you are weighing Lenin Peak against Aconcagua, you can think of the difference this way: Aconcagua, 6,962 m, is slightly lower, and its normal route involves no roped climbing, but its wind and cold are very harsh. On Lenin Peak you cross a crevassed glacier and sections with fixed ropes, and you sleep above 6,000 m. With us, Aconcagua requires previous experience at an altitude of at least 5,000 m, and Lenin Peak experience above 5,500 m. We set out the Aconcagua normal route, camp by camp, in a separate guide.

Good to know: the climb is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides. In the mountains there is no promise of a summit, only a commitment to safety.
Lenin Peak with HighAir

Our Lenin Peak expedition lasts 20 days, departs in July and August, and is limited to 12 participants. The price is 6,200 US dollars per person, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 68 percent.

The price includes airport to hotel transfers and internal transfers, one night in a hotel in Osh with breakfast, tent accommodation throughout the climb, 3 full meals a day throughout the climb, professional local English-speaking guides, porters carrying up to 25 kg of personal gear to Base Camp and up to 15 kg between the camps, use of showers, toilets, laundry and electricity at the camps, reserve entry permits and the Lenin Peak climbing permit, a Magnus satellite device for the group, a personal gear checklist with an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide, a personal area in the HighAir app, and a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance, lunch and dinner at the hotel in Osh, personal gear (clothing, footwear and mountaineering boots), climbing gear (crampons, ice axe, harness, ropes and carabiners), tips for guides and porters (250 US dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (600 US dollars per person) and personal expenses such as internet, alcohol, a yurt upgrade and sauna. Optional extras: an extra day at Base Camp (50 US dollars per person) and an extra day at the high camps (150 US dollars per person). In the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Everyone who has stood on a summit above 7,000 meters got there step by step, and mountain by mountain. If your previous mountain is already behind you and Lenin Peak is next, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does it take to climb Lenin Peak?

On the HighAir expedition the whole journey lasts 20 days, from arrival in Osh to the flight home. The itinerary includes acclimatization days at Base Camp, an acclimatization rotation up to Camp 3 at 6,100 m, two rest days, a summit day and a spare day for bad weather.
What experience do I need to climb Lenin Peak?

Previous experience above 5,500 m is required, for example on Kilimanjaro or Aconcagua. The mountain is not very technical, but it requires very high endurance and the ability to cope with significant altitude conditions. A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure.
Do I need crampons, an ice axe and ropes on Lenin Peak?

Yes. The route crosses a crevassed glacier and steep sections, and you work with crampons, an ice axe, a harness, ropes and carabiners. On day 6 there is ice training and preparation for the climb at Camp 1. Climbing gear is not included in the price of the expedition.
Do I need a visa for Kyrgyzstan?

Citizens of the UK, the US, the EU and many other countries enter Kyrgyzstan without a visa for a stay of up to 30 days (as of 2026). The Base Camp area also requires a border zone permit, which is arranged in advance. Entry rules can change, so check them for your passport before booking and again before you fly.
When is the season for climbing Lenin Peak?
The climbing season is summer, mainly July and August, when the camps at the foot of the mountain operate and the weather is more stable. Our expeditions depart in July and August.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains.
